lesson.title: Right Triangle Geometry: The Pythagorean Theorem in Action
lesson.summary: In any right triangle, the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides, a relationship called the Pythagorean theorem that lets you find any missing side once you know the other two.
lesson.body:
A right triangle has one 90 degree angle, and the three sides around it have specific names. The two sides that form the right angle are called legs, and the side opposite the right angle, always the longest side in the triangle, is called the hypotenuse. This labeling matters because the relationship between these sides is not arbitrary, it is one of the most reliable facts in all of geometry: if a and b are the lengths of the two legs and c is the length of the hypotenuse, then a squared plus b squared equals c squared. This is the Pythagorean theorem, and it holds for every right triangle, no matter how large, small, or oddly proportioned.

The reason this relationship is so useful on the ACT is that it turns a triangle with a missing side into a straightforward algebra problem: plug in the two lengths you know, and solve for the one you do not, using the same equation-solving instincts from the earlier chapters in this course.

Suppose a right triangle has legs of length 6 and 8, and you need the hypotenuse. Set up the theorem: 6 squared plus 8 squared equals c squared, so 36 plus 64 equals c squared, giving 100 equals c squared. Taking the square root of both sides, c equals 10. This particular triangle, with sides 6, 8, and 10, is a scaled up version of the smaller 3, 4, 5 triangle, and recognizing these common Pythagorean triples, along with others like 5, 12, 13, can save real time on a timed test since you can skip the square root step entirely once you spot the pattern.

Right triangles are not just a geometry curiosity, they are the setting for the next chapter, trigonometry. Once you are comfortable finding a missing side with the Pythagorean theorem, the natural next question is how the angles of a right triangle relate to the ratios of its sides, which is exactly what sine, cosine, and tangent describe. The 6, 8, 10 triangle from this example will reappear in the next chapter for precisely that reason.
